title: Google Makes School Search and AI Off by Default — and Schools Still Cannot Get Search Without AI
excerpt: Google said Tuesday it will switch off Search, Gemini and its classroom AI tools by default for K-12 student accounts until an administrator opts in. After a backlash, it clarified schools can decline Gemini and keep Search — but Search itself now comes with AI Overviews that cannot be switched off.
body:
• Google said on Tuesday it will by default turn off its AI tools, including Search and the Gemini chatbot, for K-12 student accounts; an administrator must explicitly enable them.
  • Administrators who switch Search on can also enable a guided learning mode, which detects pasted schoolwork questions and walks students through problems step by step instead of giving the answer.
  • The first version of the policy drew charges of coercion — Senator Bernie Sanders called it extortion — and Google clarified within hours that schools can decline the Gemini products and keep Search: the controls are separate.
  • What has not changed: there is no AI-free Search. A school that enables Search gets AI Overviews and AI Mode with it, and Google offers no way to disable just the AI features. Rollout details are still to come over the coming months; nothing has yet taken effect.

Google has redrawn how its products reach schoolchildren, and then redrawn part of the redraw within a day. The company said on Tuesday it will by default turn off its AI tools, including Search and the Gemini chatbot, for primary and secondary (K-12) student accounts, according to The Wall Street Journal. Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Gemini in Classroom are covered by the same default. Nothing changes until a school administrator explicitly enables each tool.

The version that caused the backlash

The controversy was over what happened to schools that said no. Google vice president for education Chris Phillips had told The New York Times that Search and AI are deeply integrated, and that students at schools rejecting AI would lose Search and see an unavailable notice. The reaction was immediate: former FTC chair Lina Khan called it using a search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI; Senator Bernie Sanders called it extortion; New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said corporations should not dictate how children are taught. Rohit Chopra, the former FTC commissioner now serving as California Business and Consumer Services Agency secretary, said big tech giants should not be able to strong-arm schools or use kids as subjects in their experiments.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DeSuiavml1p/

"They are separate controls."

— Google spokesman Davis Thompson, confirming schools can decline Gemini and keep Search, via Superpower Daily

The clarification, and the catch that survives it

Google then clarified, through spokesman Davis Thompson, that schools can decline the Gemini products and keep Search — the two are separate admin controls, Superpower Daily reported, synthesising the Mercury News and Bloomberg coverage. But one element of the original position stands: there is no AI-free Search. Districts that enable Search cannot fully turn off the AI Overviews and AI Mode that now ship inside it; Google says AI is integral to Search and offers no switch for the AI features alone. A school that wants zero AI still faces the choice the critics objected to.

Why Google moved at all

The default-off shift follows pressure from two directions. A September Wall Street Journal investigation, based on more than 60 interviews, found some students becoming emotionally and academically dependent on Google classroom AI; in late October, Senators Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley wrote to chief executive Sundar Pichai expressing grave concern. Google education chief Phillips wrote in the company blog post that Google will continue to listen to feedback and evolve its approach in partnership with schools, teachers, pedagogical experts and parents. Rollout specifics are promised over the coming months, and nothing has yet taken effect — which means districts, and parents, have a window to ask their schools which way the new switches will be set.
